newsitem.title: UK: Shorts and longs meet on LME zinc battleground.
newsitem.headline: Shorts and longs meet on LME zinc battleground.

text.p: Funds and other speculative buyers jumped in on the back of LME zinc's continued rise as most longs continued an aggressive squeeze of Chinese shorts.
The market looked set for a further spike, and traders said they expected a rise in the short-term to $1,800 per tonne, basis 3-months and $2,000 for cash zinc.
Zinc reached almost $1,675 per tonne on Monday after a Friday kerb close at $1,624 which was capped by profit taking.
"Once a squeeze is in place it tends to work on itself, particularly if the fundamentals suggest that intervention by the LME may not be warranted," said analyst Larry Kaplan of Flemings Research.

Chinese short covering was just one of the driving forces of a metal which has taken the base metals complex by storm, fuelling rises for other metals such as copper which is not fundamentally bullish, said traders.

"There is fresh fund and speculative buying, pushing prices higher," a trader said, adding that "the Chinese will have to deliver some portion of their position, but most of it has already been done."
Physical consumers who had anticipated a quiet summer for zinc may also need to restock, giving zinc a further boost in the fourth quarter, Kaplan said.
The market was divided on how much of the Chinese smelters' short position was actually covered.
Traders said the Chinese were reported to have used a combination of covering and rolling over rather than squaring up completely.

The difficulties of the Chinese smelters were mainly due to bad timing, according to Robin Bhar of LME brokers Brandeis, who said that much of the loss-making Chinese futures position was offset by physical business.
"The Chinese have already exported a lot of material at prevailing LME prices," Bhar said.

He added that by using material from the Huladao smelter, stockpiled zinc and by selling high grade (HG) material domestically to keep super high grade (SHG) for the international market, the Chinese shorts would be able to meet their delivery commitments in September.

The China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC) said it would coordinate different smelters in an effort to deliver enough zinc to cover those Chinese smelters which are short up to 250,000 tonnes of zinc sold at $1,100 per tonne.
Chinese exports of zinc rose by 140 percent in the first half of 1997, compared with the equivalent period of 1996, to 248,829 tonnes, according to Brandeis' assessment of Chinese customs figures.
Total exports are expected to reach 480,000 tonnes, compared to the previous record of 278,000 tonnes in 1994, CNNC said.

"The battle lines between CNNC and 'Western funds' have been well and truly drawn. The Chinese promise to export huge amounts of zinc in the face of what they see as a concerted attempt by Western traders and funds to force maximum losses from their short positions," said Jim Lennon at Macquarrie Bank.

Lennon said the failure by the Chinese to obtain export licences would also be key. Some of the "panic buying" in zinc could be due to rumours of the Chinese not being allowed to export in August/September.

An off-exchange deal between the Chinese smelters and a dominant western merchant was mooted, but with bullish sentiment prevailing, the longs were likely to hang on for higher prices still, traders said.

"Ironically, current high prices are good for the Chinese. Why should they settle for an off-market deal if they can recover their losses on the physical side," said Brandeis' Bhar. He added that China may also sell copper from its strategic stockpile to help cover any futures losses.
Technical indicators continue to ring warning bells for some analysts, who predict a fall in price once the tightness eases.
"This market is becoming more overbought each day and a correction is due soon," said Harry Creates of LME dealer Amalgamated Metal Trading.

"A crash in prices appears inevitable at some stage, but, for those looking to short the market the crucial question is at what price. There still appears to be more upside, maybe even $200 per tonne," said Lennon.

"If the Chinese figures (of increased exports of zinc) are taken at face value then we would expect a sharp downward correction in prices by Q4 as the Chinese short positions are unwound," he added. - London Newsroom +44 171 542 8071
